lines: I told the apprentice to mind his temper. He put it beside the tongs.
A customer asked for a sword that never dulls. I sold him a painting of one.
The grindstone and I agree on most things. We both hate rough edges.
I made a silent weapon once. Nobody heard the complaint until the handle fell off.
A guard wanted a lighter sword, so I told him to stop filling the sheath with snacks.
The axe said it wanted a raise. I put it on a higher rack.
I asked the hammer for a second opinion. It made the same point again.
Someone requested a blade fit for a king. I asked whether the king could lift it.
The dagger claimed it was subtle. The jeweled handle disagreed.
A sword with no balance is just a long argument with your wrist.
I offered the anvil a day off. It took the news hard.
The apprentice polished one side of a blade and called the other side rustic.
A dull sword walked into the forge. It did not make much of a point.
The shield asked me for advice. I told it to stop taking everything personally.
A spear is easy to understand. It gets straight to the point.
I tried to tell a quiet joke, but the hammer finished it.
A customer asked whether the edge was sharp. His missing sleeve answered first.
The scabbard does the hardest work here. It keeps the sword out of conversations.
I forged a blade for a show-off once. The mirror finish was all he used.
An axe and a sword argued over reach. The bow laughed from across the room.
The grindstone never holds a grudge. It removes one layer at a time.
A chipped blade asked for privacy. I said the damage was already public.
The guard wanted his sword to look dangerous. I suggested he learn to hold it first.
I named a hammer Patience. Nobody enjoys being taught by it.
The best thing about a well-balanced weapon is that the owner has one less excuse.
